With Qwen3.5-9B, it reaches 83.77 and 60.9, respectively, while latency falls from 1.56 to 0.16 s. The OVO-Bench improvements appear in its Real, Backward, and Forward subsets, suggesting that the retained context remains useful for both incoming visual evidence and information from earlier video frames.

The results are particularly relevant to interactive agents, as reducing latency is only useful if the system can still interpret the observations needed for its next decision. These comparisons show that the serving optimizations do not require sacrificing the measured streaming-video accuracy on either backbone. They also establish a practical connection between efficient context reuse and the real-time policy inference used in our game experiments. Peak memory remains in the same general range as the matched-backbone baselines, with 22 GB reported for Streaming-vLLM. For OVO-Bench Forward, the latency measure excludes the time spent waiting for sufficient visual evidence, separating model computation from the benchmark’s delayed-answer protocol.

8.6.1 Inference Efficiency

We next evaluate Streaming-vLLM on the actual keyboard-mouse interaction workload used by the Verl-based training and evaluation framework. This is the inference path through which policy actions are generated for online TA-GRPO rollouts as well as real-time testing. Table 9 summarizes measured system configurations on NVIDIA H200 (Hopper) using the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE model. To evaluate transferability of the serving design beyond this one configuration, Appendix C.4 separately compares the Qwen3-VL-8B Dense model and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE model across NVIDIA A800 (Ampere) and H200 (Hopper), multiple tensor-parallel degrees, and BF16 or W8A8 precision.

The cumulative configurations cover stateful serving, tensor parallelism, operator fusion, parallel overlap, CUDA Graphs, a low-overhead execution backend, quantization, and FSM-guided decoding with BF16 target-model verification.

End-to-end performance depends on optimizing the full interaction path. Table 9 traces successive runtime configurations for the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE model on H200. The initial TP4 streaming configuration offers only a modest change in total latency relative to the TP1 baseline. Vision processing, prefill, and autoregressive decoding impose different computational and communication costs, so accelerating one component does not necessarily reduce the complete request time by the same proportion. This motivates the use of architecture-aware kernels and overlapping execution rather than relying on tensor parallelism alone. Because some configurations also change profiling boundaries, the table reports cumulative system improvements rather than isolated single-factor effects.

Cumulative runtime optimizations yield a substantial latency reduction. Operator fusion, parallel overlap, CUDA Graph replay, and the low-overhead megakernel backend progressively reduce request latency. FSM-guided drafting further shortens action generation, while BF16 target-model verification preserves the target policy’s acceptance decision. Together, these cumulative optimizations reduce end-to-end latency from approximately 1.31 s to 65 ms, which is a 20.1×\times speedup on the measured H200 MoE configuration. The largest gains emerge when the runtime addresses vision processing, context handling, and decoding as a single interactive workload. Appendix C.4 extends the system evaluation to representative Dense and MoE configurations on A800 and H200 GPUs.

The latency reduction also increases the capacity to produce executable action packets within a fixed wall-clock interval. Table 9 reports the corresponding step rate (SR) and a theoretical control rate (CR) obtained by multiplying SR by the six action blocks per packet. These are throughput-derived capacities, not direct measurements of the client’s realized game frame rate, which follows its own execution schedule. This distinction allows the system results to quantify available inference headroom without conflating request throughput with observed gameplay cadence.

9 Conclusion

Gamer learns to control diverse and complex games through a shared keyboard-and-mouse interface. It combines large-scale continued pre-training, task-conditioned supervised fine-tuning, and temporal-aware reinforcement learning to learn transferable control, long-horizon reasoning, and persistent memory. Streaming-vLLM supports both training and deployment, enabling real-time interaction and efficient online rollouts while reducing latency-induced bias in reinforcement learning. At inference time, Gamer acts through visual observations and device-level controls without privileged game state or game-engine modifications. Environment-side task verification is used separately to provide online RL rewards. These capabilities could effectively reduce development costs through automated testing, faster game iteration, and new gameplay mechanics. By supporting real-time interaction without game-specific infrastructure, Gamer offers a basis for agents that learn and improve across complex 3D games and other interactive environments.

10 Limitations and Future Work

Several main directions remain for extending Gamer’s scope and accessibility. First, our evaluation covers a selected set of environments and task structures. The shared observation-action interface provides a basis for extending joint post-training and systematic evaluation to broader interactive settings. Our preliminary results suggest the potential for improving performance and generalization by scaling relevant gameplay data across a broader range of environments. These benefits depend on the coverage and composition of the training experience.

Second, Streaming-vLLM enables real-time interaction on the evaluated GPU platforms, while further reductions in serving costs would support wider deployment. Model compression and additional runtime optimizations offer promising directions for extending this efficiency to more resource-constrained settings while preserving responsiveness and task performance.

Third, although Gamer improves the trade-off between response latency and task performance in the evaluated settings, reasoning capability may remain a bottleneck in environments that demand deeper deliberation. Fast, continuous interaction alone does not ensure the ability to solve complex strategic problems. Our framework provides a foundation for exploring hierarchical game agents that combine a larger model for deliberative System 2 reasoning with a fast model for reactive System 1 execution. Such architectures could coordinate longer-term planning with timely control, extending the range of tasks that agents can handle under real-time constraints.

Appendix A Related Work

A.1 Generalist Game Agents

Research on game-playing agents has expanded from environment-specific policies to general models combining perception, reasoning, memory, and executable control. Large-scale behavioral pretraining provides one route: VPT [4] learns Minecraft control from internet videos labeled by an inverse dynamics model, while STEVE-1 [21] extends this paradigm to language-conditioned behavior. Other systems, including DEPS [48], Voyager [44], JARVIS-1 [49], Optimus-1 [20], and OmniJARVIS [50], incorporate planning, reusable skills, and memory to support increasingly complex tasks.

Recent work further targets generalization across tasks and worlds. Gato [38] and SIMA [37] study shared policies across heterogeneous environments, while Game-TARS [51] and Lumine [41] combine reasoning, memory, and native keyboard–mouse control for extended gameplay. NitroGen [26] and OpenP2P [56] instead emphasize scalable visual policy learning from broad gameplay data. These approaches address different aspects of generalist gameplay, typically emphasizing cross-environment reactive control or extended reasoning under more specialized training settings. We combine cross-game continued pre-training with task-oriented policy optimization for sustained interaction.

A.2 Scalable Gameplay Learning

Progress in game agents increasingly relies on large and heterogeneous interaction data. MineRL [14] and MineDojo [11] provide structured demonstrations and multimodal resources, while VPT [4] scales behavioral learning through inverse dynamics. D2E [8], NitroGen [26], and OpenP2P [56] broaden supervision through desktop trajectories, visible control overlays, and inverse-dynamics-labeled gameplay. GameHorizon [47] further introduces multi-level annotations spanning operations, subgoals, and strategies.

Transfer also depends on model size and data composition. General scaling and continual-pretraining studies show that performance depends jointly on model capacity, data budget, and domain mixture. In gameplay, VPT [4] demonstrates the value of large-scale behavioral pretraining, while OpenP2P [56] studies scaling through both predictive performance and causal behavior. GameScaling varies model size, interaction budget, and game composition to distinguish between gains obtained by learning a shared control interface and gains that depend on target-relevant gameplay. Scale alone is not sufficient for task-oriented gameplay. Effective policy learning also requires supervision that connects local actions with higher-level objectives. GameHorizon [47] introduces temporal hierarchy into gameplay supervision, while OmniJARVIS [50] and Lumine [41] combine reasoning, memory, and staged training. We train the policy with supervision at the operation, subgoal, and task levels, and retain compact task summaries across context boundaries.

A.3 Memory and Long-Horizon Interaction

Sustained gameplay also requires agents to retain task-relevant information after earlier interactions leave the active context. Existing agents address this through reusable skills, retrieved experience, or compressed interaction histories. Voyager stores executable skills, JARVIS-1 [49] and Optimus-1 [20] retrieve accumulated experience, and Game-TARS [51] combines recent interactions with compressed textual history. OmniJARVIS [50] and Lumine [41] further integrate memory with reasoning and action generation. We explicitly supervise task summaries and use them as persistent task state during supervised training, online policy optimization, and streaming inference.

Feedback-based optimization provides a complementary mechanism for improving extended behavior. GRPO [39] optimizes relative advantages across groups of sampled outputs, while GUI-R1 [24] and Game-RL [42] adapt reinforcement learning to executable GUI actions and multimodal game reasoning. Game-TARS [51] also refines thought–action trajectories through action-consistency-based filtering. We optimize finite trajectory segments linked by compressed memory, updating task-state maintenance and executable behavior together. Long-horizon interaction must also operate under bounded context and latency. StreamingLLM [53] maintains stable inference with a fixed attention window, while InfiniPot-V [15], DSCache [34], and StreamingVLM [54] explore compressed or structured memory for continuous visual streams. Serving techniques such as PagedAttention [16] and speculative decoding further reduce autoregressive inference cost. These directions are largely studied separately from long-horizon policy optimization. Our streaming engine uses bounded memory, cache reuse, and the task representation learned during training to sustain interaction within context and latency limits.

Gamer combines cross-game behavioral scaling, multi-level task supervision, and memory-supported long-horizon interaction in one policy.

Appendix B CPT Scaling and Cross-Game Generalization

B.1 Data Mixtures and Validation Distributions

The controlled CPT grid holds its source inventory fixed while varying the share of Minecraft trajectories. S1 uses Minecraft exclusively. S2-S4 draw from the same 80 canonical game labels with different sampling weights, and S5 removes Minecraft, leaving 79 labels. You can find more details in Table 10. Consequently, the five mixtures should not be interpreted as a monotonic increase in the number of game worlds. We summarize diversity using the effective number of worlds, exp(−∑wpwlogpw)\exp(-\sum_{w}p_{w}\log p_{w}), which accounts for the balance of gameplay samples across game labels.

The fixed non-Minecraft pool contains 124 source-stream labels mapping to 79 canonical game labels. The three validation distributions separate Minecraft held-out clips, training-covered game clips, and title-disjoint unseen-game clips. The latter is game-balanced, with 28 unseen titles and 160 clips per title (4,480 clips in total). Grouping by source recording and removing title aliases limit overlap between training and validation. These splits distinguish transfer of the action interface from gains limited to games in the training mixture.

B.2 Scaling Results from GameScaling

This subsection collects the scaling results from GameScaling [58] summarized in Sec. 8.2. These results characterize how model size, gameplay budget, and game composition affect CPT within the evaluated configurations and provide context for Gamer’s CPT stage.

Interface adaptation.

Figure 12 reports keyboard, mouse, and action-format losses together with directional prediction accuracy. The rapid early decrease in these losses and the improvement in directional accuracy suggest that initial CPT learning partly concerns adaptation to the shared keyboard-mouse interface.

Training and validation losses.

Figure 13 reports training loss and validation losses on Minecraft, other training games, and unseen games. The curves show that gains from additional gameplay data depend on model capacity and game composition. In particular, validation loss on distant unseen games plateaus or increases after early adaptation, even while training loss continues to decrease.

Gameplay benchmark performance.

Figure 14 reports performance on MCU, ViZDoom, OmniGameArena, and GameWorld under time-paused interaction. These results complement the validation-loss analysis with executable gameplay outcomes. Within the evaluated configurations, mixed-game training supports transfer to related environments, while gains on more distant games remain limited.

B.3 Composition-Aware Scaling-Law Fitting

This subsection summarizes the fitting procedure and results reported in GameScaling [58], using the notation of Sec. 2.3. The composition-aware scaling relation is fitted separately to Minecraft validation loss and validation loss over the remaining training-game distribution:

ℒval​(N,D,q)=E+CNNa+CD​qηDb+Cq(q+ϵ)c.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(N,D,q)=E+\frac{C_{N}}{N^{a}}+\frac{C_{D}q^{\eta}}{D^{b}}+\frac{C_{q}}{(q+\epsilon)^{c}}. (17)

The fitted parameter vector is

ϕ=(E,CN,CD,Cq,a,b,c,η,ϵ).\bm{\phi}=\left(E,C_{N},C_{D},C_{q},a,b,c,\eta,\epsilon\right).

Model size NN is measured in billions of parameters and data budget DD in hours of gameplay interaction. For Minecraft validation, we use

q=wMC,q=w_{\mathrm{MC}},

where wMCw_{\mathrm{MC}} is the Minecraft fraction of the gameplay mixture. For validation over the other training games, we use

q=1−wMC.q=1-w_{\mathrm{MC}}.

The complete fit uses the 120 controlled configurations described in Sec. 8.2. All validation losses are measured from checkpoints that complete the corresponding training budget and decay phase.

Fitting objective. Let 𝒥fit\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{fit}} denote the set of configurations used for fitting and let LjobsL_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}} denote the observed validation loss of configuration jj. We define the log residual as

ej​(ϕ)=log⁡ℒval​(Nj,Dj,qj,ϕ)−log⁡Ljobs.e_{j}(\bm{\phi})=\log\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\left(N_{j},D_{j},q_{j},\bm{\phi}\right)-\log L_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}.

The fitted parameters minimize a Huber objective:

ϕ⋆=arg⁡min⁡∑j∈𝒥fitϕ⁡hδ​(ej​(ϕ)),\bm{\phi}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\bm{\phi}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{fit}}}h_{\delta}\left(e_{j}(\bm{\phi})\right), (18)

where hδh_{\delta} is quadratic for small residuals and linear for large residuals. We use δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}. The logarithmic residual emphasizes relative prediction error, while the Huber objective reduces sensitivity to individual outlier configurations.

We optimize Eq. (18) with L-BFGS-B [5] and retain the solution with the lowest objective among 192 initializations. The positive scale parameters EE, CNC_{N}, CDC_{D}, and CqC_{q} are optimized in log space. We constrain

a,b∈[0,3],η∈[−3,3],c∈[0,5],ϵ∈[10−4,1].a,b\in[0,3],\qquad\eta\in[-3,3],\qquad c\in[0,5],\qquad\epsilon\in[10^{-4},1].

Fitted parameters. Table 11 reports the point estimates obtained from the complete controlled grid.

Block-wise holdout evaluation. To evaluate predictive performance beyond the configurations used for fitting, we remove complete blocks of model sizes, data budgets, or game mixtures. For each holdout setting, the scaling relation is refit using the remaining configurations, and RMSE is computed only over the held-out block. The holdout results show that predictions over model size and interaction budget remain accurate near the measured range. Mixture prediction is more sensitive to the availability of nearby compositions, particularly for Minecraft when S4 is held out.

Different parameter combinations can produce similar loss surfaces, making it hard to identify individual exponents and offsets separately. The predicted loss surface is substantially more stable than the individual fitted parameters. We therefore assess the relation using the observed scaling curves, within-mixture explanatory power, and block-wise holdout error, without relying on any single coefficient.

We additionally estimate fitting uncertainty using 300 stratified bootstrap resamples within each game mixture. These intervals characterize uncertainty conditional on the observed training runs and do not include variation across independent training seeds.

B.4 Scaling Robustness and Predictive Uncertainty

The composition-aware relation explains both differences among mixtures and their different slopes with respect to gameplay hours. An equally parameterized categorical-offset alternative cannot predict a held-out mixture and yields higher training-grid errors: Minecraft RMSE 0.0044 versus 0.0020 and in-corpus RMSE 0.0035 versus 0.0012. By contrast, distant unseen-game losses generally rise after the early interface phase, and their within-mixture scaling fit is weak. We therefore interpret the fitted relation as an empirical description of the measured in-corpus data regime rather than a universal law for unseen environments. Figure 15 and Table 12 demonstrate the fit’s accuracy and limitations.

B.5 Frontier-Model Progress and CPT Transfer

Figure 16 places the GameScaling CPT checkpoints alongside successive general-purpose model releases on MCU, ViZDoom, OmniGameArena, and GameWorld. The controlled GameScaling results show that gameplay pretraining enables smaller backbones to achieve substantial gains on the source and related 3D environments. However, improvements across generations of general-purpose models are also pronounced, particularly on GameWorld, where distant-world transfer remains limited for the CPT checkpoints. The trends reflect progress from both game-specific adaptation and improvements to the underlying multimodal model. All points in this comparison use time-paused evaluation, so they characterize gameplay capability without conflating it with the real-time latency effects examined in the main experiments.

B.6 Test-Time Interaction Budgets

As illustrated in Figure 17, increasing the test-time budget from 600 to 3,000 steps raises success for the CPT models in this comparison. The two reported checkpoints reach 59.3% and 69.3% at 3,000 steps, while the unadapted backbones remain near zero. A larger interaction budget helps policies that have already learned useful control, but cannot replace CPT. These curves are supplementary to the fixed-budget primary MCU scores.

Appendix C Streaming-vLLM Implementation Details

C.1 FSM-Guided Drafting and BF16 Verification

FSM grammar coverage. The SM90 fast FSM recognizes the boundaries <think>, </think>, <|action_start|>, and <|action_end|>. It can draft the end of an empty reasoning span or the beginning of an action packet after a finished reasoning span. Within the XYZ mouse-coordinate fields, the FSM drafts formatting tokens following numerical values, not the coordinate values themselves. In the six subsequent key groups, it drafts predictable delimiters, blank-key templates, and the action terminator. Candidate tokens are proposed opportunistically when the current grammar state supports them.

Target-model verification. The drafts are checked by the BF16 target model before being committed. Under greedy decoding, only a candidate prefix that agrees with target-model token selection is accepted. Rejected suffixes and their speculative cache states are discarded. FSM output is therefore a fast proposal, not constrained decoding or a replacement for the policy’s action decisions. The implementation should report the drafting window, prefix acceptance, and verified output consistency under the selected inference configuration.

Stochastic decoding. If stochastic sampling is used, preserving the target sampling distribution requires a proposal-aware acceptance rule and residual correction rather than unconditionally accepting FSM predictions [17]. We do not assume that such a correction is enabled in every deployment configuration. The SM90 results correspond to the implemented BF16 target-model verification path. Distribution-preserving stochastic decoding requires the appropriate acceptance rule.

C.2 Incremental RoPE Cache Refresh

Figure 18 illustrates the incremental positional refresh used for retained KV states after context compaction. A cached key originally associated with logical position pp may be reassigned to a new position p^\widehat{p}. Rather than recomputing its key projection, Streaming-vLLM applies only the positional difference

Δ​p=p^−p.\Delta p=\widehat{p}-p.

For a pair of cached key components (u,v)(u,v) associated with rotary frequency ωi\omega_{i}, let

ϕ=Δ​p​ωi.\phi=\Delta p\,\omega_{i}.

The incremental update is implemented as

u′\displaystyle u^{\prime} =u​cos⁡ϕ−v​sin⁡ϕ,\displaystyle=u\cos\phi-v\sin\phi, (19)
v′\displaystyle v^{\prime} =u​sin⁡ϕ+v​cos⁡ϕ.\displaystyle=u\sin\phi+v\cos\phi.

Both updated components are computed from the original pair before being written back to the cache. The implementation follows the component-pair layout used by the underlying model and applies the corresponding update independently to all dimensions participating in RoPE.

Tokens whose logical positions remain unchanged have Δ​p=0\Delta p=0 and therefore require no modification. The update is performed in place on the retained key cache. No unrotated key representation is stored, and the value cache is left unchanged. For RoPE variants with multiple positional axes, the same correction is applied independently to the component groups associated with each axis.

This update corrects only the rotary positional phase. As discussed in Sec. 5.1, retained KV states continue to follow the stateful streaming semantics of Streaming-vLLM rather than being reconstructed through full re-encoding after memory compaction.

C.3 Hardware and Model-Architecture Coverage

Hardware mapping and evaluated backbones. The Ampere measurements use NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while the Hopper measurements use NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Figure 19 compares Qwen3-VL-8B, a representative dense visual-language model, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, a representative mixture-of-experts model. Both are run with multiple tensor-parallel configurations and numerical precision settings. The Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 families are supported at additional dense and MoE sizes listed in Table 15, but this figure should not be read as an exhaustive per-checkpoint benchmark.

Representative cross-hardware behavior. Under TP4 and BF16, Qwen3-VL-8B has a mean request latency of 147.64 ms on A800 and 75.66 ms on H200. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B has corresponding latencies of 205.77 ms and 110.08 ms. On H200, TP4 FP8 W8A8 further yields 74.69 ms and 92.19 ms, respectively. These figures come from the existing latency-composition sweep and are not matched compute-cost comparisons across GPU generations. These results show that the same stateful serving design supports dense and MoE backbones on both architectures. The best parallelism and precision settings vary with the model and hardware.

C.4 Latency Composition and Control-Rate Interpretation

The end-to-end request time comprises vision encoding, context processing, action generation, and runtime overhead. In the figure, Ampere denotes NVIDIA A800, and Hopper denotes NVIDIA H200. Figure 19 compares these components across model architectures, hardware generations, parallel settings, and numerical precision. The system ablation reports step rate (SR), the reciprocal of end-to-end request latency, and a theoretical control rate (CR) obtained by multiplying SR by the six low-level blocks in each action packet. CR is a latency-derived upper bound, not a direct measurement of the client execution cadence. The latter uses approximately 33 ms per block (30 Hz) when actions arrive in time.

Appendix D Honkai: Star Rail Evaluation Protocol and Taxonomy

D.1 World Diversity and Interactive Complexity

Honkai: Star Rail provides a useful setting for studying generalist game agents because its complexity comes from combining familiar interactions across a large, varied world, rather than from a single difficult mechanic. Figure 20 brings together 171 floor maps from 85 areas across the game’s major worlds. The maps range from compact rooms and branching corridors to large open layouts, interconnected structures, and multi-floor environments. Even when presented at a common coordinate scale, their differences are apparent. An agent cannot assume that a route learned in one area will work in another. It must adjust to new geometry, identify transitions between areas or floors, and preserve its destination as the scene changes.

The many point icons also reveal how exploration and task execution are interleaved. Individual areas contain resources and other points of interest alongside locations relevant to progression and interaction. A route can pass several optional objects before reaching the target, and the shortest visible path need not be a feasible sequence of game actions. The red paths in Figure 20 are schematic exploration routes, not gameplay-verified optimal solutions. They illustrate the need to plan through branching spaces, but do not establish that any particular route is the fastest or most reliable. The annotated maps are provided only to describe the environment and are not given to the evaluated agents as observations or privileged navigation input.

Accessible gameplay does not imply easy autonomous control. For a human player, quest objectives, map markers, and familiar interaction prompts make many individual steps understandable. A vision-language-action agent receives only the rendered screen and must turn this guidance into timed keyboard and mouse inputs. It must recognize where it is, distinguish relevant objects from nearby distractions, navigate while the camera and scene change, and determine when an interaction has actually completed. Longer tasks add another difficulty: navigation, dialogue, UI manipulation, combat, and local puzzles may appear within the same quest. Failure at one step can invalidate a later plan, and an agent must remember earlier progress even after those observations leave its active context. The challenge is therefore not simply to play any one minigame, but to coordinate heterogeneous skills over time.

This combination makes the game useful for both research and practical evaluation. Short interactive challenges probe whether a policy can adapt to different local rules, while side quests test whether those skills support sustained, instruction-conditioned progress. The same interface also reflects conditions faced by automated game testing: new content introduces routes, objects, objectives, and mechanics that cannot all be anticipated by hand-written scripts. A generalist agent able to execute these tasks through screen observations and device-level actions could support exploration, quest verification, and regression testing without modifications to the game engine. These are potential applications, not deployment benefits measured by the map itself. Our experiments cover a defined subset of this broader environment. Although Gamer-CPT is trained on other Honkai: Star Rail gameplay, neither of the two evaluated side quests nor any of the 40 scored minigame tasks is included in training. This split tests generalization to held-out tasks within a familiar game world, not zero-shot transfer to a game unseen during training.

D.2 Combat Mechanics and Strategic Decision-Making

Exploration is only one part of Honkai: Star Rail. Combat adds a different decision-making problem within the same game interface. The game uses turn-based encounters, but choosing an action still depends on information that changes throughout the fight. As shown in Figure 21, the combat screen combines the action-order queue with character HP, enemy Toughness, team status, skill points, and available abilities. The action-order display and Action Value indicate when combatants will act, while the Toughness system creates opportunities for Weakness Break. The agent must use these cues together, rather than treating each turn as an isolated image-to-action decision.

Combat decisions involve coupled constraints over multiple turns. Attacking a vulnerable target may advance a Weakness Break, but the agent must also consider the available skill points, the health and status of its team, and which combatant acts next. Character roles introduce further variation. The Paths shown in Figure 21 span single-target and multi-target damage, buffs and debuffs, protection and healing, summons, and other specialized combat effects. A useful action can therefore depend on the team composition and on how one character’s choice changes the options available to others. Although human players can read these cues from a familiar interface, an autonomous policy must recognize them visually, choose a suitable action, and issue the corresponding executable inputs.

This makes combat complementary to the game’s navigation, dialogue, and puzzle mechanics. Navigation requires spatial grounding and route execution, whereas combat requires state-dependent target selection and coordination of limited resources across turns. Both demand that the agent preserve its objective while the available actions and relevant observations change. The held-out side-quest benchmark includes combat milestones alongside other interaction types. The atlas in Figure 21 provides context for those milestones and the broader game setting, rather than constituting a separate combat benchmark or evidence of a model’s combat performance. Together with the exploration maps, it illustrates why generalist gameplay requires more than a collection of fixed action scripts: the same visual-control policy must adapt to different rules, time scales, and notions of progress within one evolving game world.

D.3 Long-Horizon Milestones

The long-horizon benchmark consists of two fixed quest specifications. Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) contains 30 evaluation milestones grouped into 22 parent steps, with 14 navigation, 14 dialogue, one combat, and one UI milestone. Bestial Ferocity contains 55 milestones grouped into 40 parent steps, with 32 navigation, 16 dialogue, two combat, two UI, and three puzzle milestones. Configured time budgets are attached to each required milestone. They are limits for evaluation, not observations of how long an agent took to complete a step. The ordering and terminal conditions are listed in Tables 13 and 14.

For each model, the milestone-type rate is the number of verified passes divided by the total milestones of that type in the respective quest. Quest accuracy uses all required milestones as its denominator rather than averaging type-level rates. If a run resumes through a scripted transition, a verified milestone pass does not establish uninterrupted autonomous progress. Missing evaluations are not counted as failures. The published report should state the exact number of valid attempts per model and task when final results are available.

D.4 Minigame Coverage and Visualization

The scored minigame benchmark contains 40 tasks across seven types: Magflow Link (ML), Navigation Compass (NC), Abacus Circuitry (AC), Hexanexus (HX), Janus’s Hidden Passage (JHP), Golden Scapegoat (GS), and Janus’s Maze (JM). The extended gallery in Figure 22 illustrates other mechanics encountered in the game, but those examples are not additional scored types in the reported benchmark. Capability tags describe the main reasoning or control challenge for visualization and do not enter the accuracy calculation. Understanding diverse and complex gameplay mechanics is essential for general game agents, as modern commercial games such as Honkai: Star Rail typically combine multiple mechanics within a single game.

We compute accuracy by first averaging the success outcomes of valid attempts for each task, then averaging task scores within each game type, and finally taking an unweighted mean over the seven type-level scores. Unlike an any-success-at-three metric, this score retains fractional success rates when a task succeeds in only a subset of its attempts. The seven-type macro-average prevents categories with more tasks from dominating the result.

Extended Main-Story Evaluation.

Beyond side quests and minigames, we further evaluate Gamer on the main storyline of Honkai: Star Rail, covering five major story arcs with 19 quest chains and 160 main-story mission entries. Across approximately 50 hours of gameplay evaluation, our model operates autonomously for over 95% of the total evaluation time, demonstrating sustained gameplay proficiency across diverse environments, complex interactions, and long sequences of evolving objectives. This result highlights the potential of generalist game agents to support extended autonomous gameplay beyond isolated benchmark tasks. With further reinforcement learning and model scaling, generalist game agents could serve as foundational tools for large-scale automated evaluation and testing of large modern games.

Appendix E Rollout Visualization and Qualitative Case Study

The reward curves in Figure 11 show how policy optimization progresses during training. To complement these aggregate measurements, we visualize how navigation and target interaction change across checkpoints. We compare the SFT initialization (CP 0) with five TA-GRPO checkpoints on a training task and a held-out development task. Each checkpoint is evaluated in 16 attempts from the same task and initial scene. The Task successes value on the left of each row reports the number of successful attempts, while twelve ordered frames depict one representative rollout. Executed actions and selected translated reasoning excerpts appear below the frames. The two views are complementary. The counts summarize reliability across attempts, and the screenshots make route selection, obstacle handling, and goal interaction easier to inspect.

Training rollout: Reach Pom-Pom. Figure 23 follows the policy through a multi-level interior with railings, corridors, and nearby interactable objects. The number of successful attempts grows from 3/16 for the SFT initialization to 14/16 at CP 20 and 15/16 at both CP 40 and CP 50. In the illustrated CP 20 rollout, the policy takes a route around the bar and completes the target interaction in 38.3 s. Later checkpoints also complete the displayed task. This case illustrates a useful progression from recognizing the destination to navigating the intervening geometry and executing the interaction that verifies completion. The visual examples and aggregated attempts together indicate more reliable goal-directed behavior after online training.

Development rollout: Reach March 7th. Figure 24 examines whether similar behavior emerges on a held-out navigation objective. Successful attempts increase from 1/16 at the SFT initialization to 8/16 at CP 20 and 10/16 at CP 50. The illustrated CP 20 policy follows the lower street, navigates around a pillar, and initiates the required dialogue in 46.1 s. CP 40 and CP 50 also complete the target interaction in their displayed rollouts. Because this task is not the RL training objective, the comparison provides complementary evidence that the learned navigation behavior can extend to a different destination and interaction sequence within the same game.

Across both cases, the increase in successful attempts is accompanied by more goal-directed behavior in the illustrated trajectories. Later policies more consistently select routes around obstacles, avoid unrelated interactions, and carry through to the final task-verifying action rather than stopping near the target location. The 16-attempt counts quantify the change in completion reliability, while the examples help interpret what that improvement looks like during execution. Together with the held-out side-quest results, they illustrate how online training can strengthen navigation and sustained goal pursuit.

Appendix F Training Recipe and Reproducibility Details

F.1 Unified Verl-Based Training and Inference

We extend Verl [40] to use a shared game-interaction interface across CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO. The training framework handles the stage-specific objectives and model updates, while Streaming-vLLM supplies autoregressive policy inference for interactive evaluation and online RL rollouts. The stages share the keyboard-mouse action grammar, observation-action history representation, and game-facing execution interface. CPT and SFT learn from recorded trajectories under their respective objectives, and TA-GRPO receives environment-verifiable feedback from interactions generated by the current policy. Consequently, the final policy is evaluated through the same type of executable control path used to collect online training experience.

Consistency scope. The system keeps action serialization, token boundaries, and environment timing consistent between training-stage evaluation and online policy interaction. It does not imply that every forward pass uses the same numerical kernel or cached context. Training computes gradients on supervised or rollout-derived sequences, whereas Streaming-vLLM uses stateful KV reuse, memory compaction, and architecture-dependent serving kernels. The RoPE phase adjustment in Appendix C.2 corrects retained cache positions but does not reconstruct the output of a fully re-encoded context. Consistency therefore refers to the policy interface and interaction semantics, not bitwise equality of training and inference logits.

F.2 Training Configuration and Data Separation

Controlled CPT configurations. The scaling study consists of four backbone sizes, five game mixtures, and six completed training budgets. It uses twenty primary Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) trunks, one per size-mixture pair. The shorter-budget checkpoints branch from their shared trunk and complete an independent decay phase within the stated total budget, yielding 120 evaluated configurations. All controlled runs use an 85% gameplay and 15% general vision-language token ratio, which is also retained for the separately trained HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT checkpoint. The CPT recipe uses BF16 AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, weight decay 0.010.01, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and peak learning rates of 10−510^{-5} for the language model and 7×10−67\times 10^{-6} for the unfrozen vision encoder. The WSD allocation is 3% warmup, 87.3% stable training, and 9.7% cosine decay. The controlled grid uses 854×\times480 observations, twenty visual turns per context, and approximately 2.3×1052.3\times 10^{5} supervised target tokens per update.

Cross-stage implementation. The same autoregressive device-level action representation is retained in CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO, while instruction and memory conditioning are added in the later stages. The full stage-by-stage recipe, including the image resolution actually configured for each stage, is summarized in Table 15. For the real-time RL stage, the rollout-worker and training configuration are recorded separately from the controlled CPT grid. The short-term history uses 20 dialogue turns, the memory budget is 512 tokens, and each TA-GRPO segment is bounded by 20 dialogue turns with temporal factor β=0.9\beta=0.9.

Evaluation separation. Training/validation/test splits are defined at the complete recording or task-source level before extracting overlapping action windows or multi-level examples. For interaction benchmarks, time-paused (TP) evaluation freezes the simulated environment during policy inference, whereas real-time (RT) evaluation lets the environment advance. These settings use the same action serialization but different timing semantics. Real-time performance comparisons should therefore report both the serving configuration and environment timing rather than treating model size or score as a proxy for latency.

F.3 Execution Protocol and Reproducibility

Rollout and evaluation protocol. Interactive inference produces six keyboard-mouse control blocks from the current visual observation, task instruction, and memory context. The client executes these blocks while the environment continues to advance. Online RL runs across 32 parallel game environments served by a sharded Streaming-vLLM pool with 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each iteration gathers 128 rollouts in groups of eight from the active navigation or puzzle task pool. Two disjoint rollout subsets support the policy updates, and environment task verification provides rewards without a learned process reward model. SFT and RL evaluations use matched task initializations, milestone verifiers, action semantics, and inference settings as described in Sec. 8.3.

Reproducibility boundary. After the two policy updates, the resulting checkpoint is synchronized across the inference services, and the next rollout iteration starts only after the workers acknowledge the expected policy version. Our run audit records the trainer and inference revisions, checkpoints, action serialization, tokenizer, image preprocessing, and environment settings. Inference uses BF16 with a maximum generation length of 512 tokens and temperature 0.9. The game screenshots are captured at 1280×7201280\times 720 and resized to 854×480854\times 480 for model input. TA-GRPO uses 20-turn segments and temporal factor β=0.9\beta=0.9. These settings, together with the checkpoint and service synchronization protocol, specify the interaction conditions used in the reported experiments.
